column3: What then shall we say that Abraham our forefather according to the flesh has found?
For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about—but not before God.
For what does Scripture say? “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness.”
Now to the one who works, the wage is not counted according to grace but according to what is owed.
But to the one who does not work but believes in the one who justifies the ungodly, that person’s faith is counted as righteousness,
just as David also speaks of the blessedness of the person to whom God counts righteousness apart from works:
“Blessed are those whose lawless deeds were forgiven and whose sins were covered;
blessed is the man whose sin the Lord will certainly not count.”
Is this blessedness, then, for the circumcised or also for the uncircumcised? For we say, “Faith was counted to Abraham as righteousness.”
How then was it counted? While he was circumcised or uncircumcised? Not while circumcised, but while uncircumcised.

And he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith he had while uncircumcised, so that he might be the father of all who believe while uncircumcised, so that righteousness might also be counted to them,
and the father of the circumcised, to those not only from circumcision but also walking in the footsteps of the faith our father Abraham had while uncircumcised.
For the promise to Abraham or to his offspring that he would be heir of the world was not through law, but through the righteousness of faith.
For if those from law are heirs, faith has been emptied and the promise has been nullified.
For the law produces wrath, but where there is no law there is also no transgression.

For this reason it is from faith, so that it may be according to grace, in order that the promise may be certain to all the offspring—not only to those from the law but also to those from Abraham’s faith, who is father of us all,
just as it is written, “I have appointed you father of many nations,” before the God whom he believed, the one who gives life to the dead and calls the things not existing as though they exist.
Against hope, in hope he believed, so that he might become father of many nations according to what had been said, “So shall your offspring be.”
And without becoming weak in faith, he considered his own body as good as dead, being about a hundred years old, and the deadness of Sarah’s womb.
But regarding the promise of God he did not waver in unbelief, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God
and being fully assured that what he had promised he was also able to do.
Therefore it was also counted to him as righteousness.
Now it was not written for his sake alone that it was counted to him,
but also for our sake, to whom it is about to be counted—to us who believe in the one who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead,
who was handed over because of our trespasses and was raised because of our justification.
